# What did we do on the day?

*You'll need the whole book; this chapter only explains why the day was planned as RUNBOOK says. It was written
on 4 November 2026, before the event, from what the organisers had said by then, and it gives no instruction of its
own: every instruction is RUNBOOK's, and where the two differ, RUNBOOK is right. What happened in each round is
written after the event, in the boxes marked "On the Arena".*

## The story

Qminers' own 2024 hackathon was a sports-betting contest. Its online stage ran on hidden data with a limit of 20
submissions, and one entrant scored 77,382 points, as he puts it a profit equal to the rest of the field's combined.
The final was in person, over a single Saturday: new data, scores reset to the 1,000 points everyone started with, and
a shorter horizon, "thus introducing more variance to the competition"
[(`references/qminers-hackathon-2024/README.md:33-43`)]{.src}.

Before it, he wrote a small simulation of the final: twenty finalists starting level, with models of varying quality,
correlated with each other, each with its own appetite for risk. He used it to choose how much of his bankroll to
bet, choosing the fraction that maximised his chance of winning the tournament, not his expected score
[(`README.md:45-49`)]{.src}. (The code committed for it doesn't run as it stands; the idea carries over, not the
number [(`references/wiki/sources/qminers-hackathon-2024.md`, "Traps")]{.src}.)

The final had three rounds. He took the lead in the first and extended it in the second. Before the third he worked
out that its scrambled data came from just after covid, a period other finalists' models might handle better than
his, and halved his stake so as not to lose the lead. It was, he wrote, "a minor mistake": his model "performed the
best during this time". He finished on 107,074 points, against 69,460 for the second, and estimates he would have
ended near 143,000 at full stake [(`README.md:55-63`; `final_scores.png`)]{.src}.

The point is not that halving was right. It is that the question changed once he was ahead: from "what makes the
most" to "what keeps the place".

## The idea

### How the plan was made

The plan was built in steps, each from something learned, and the dates say where each part came from
[(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "Known so far"; `IDEAS.md`, "The kickoff prompts on a disguised round")]{.src}.

- **7 October.** The organisers' e-mail gave the schedule: a playground in the morning, then four rounds of five
  hours through the night.
- **10 October.** The Arena's site, read from its own code, showed the shape of the game: one Python file uploaded
  to a web portal each round, a capped number of submissions, and public backtest data to download.
- **24 and 25 October.** We would be two, so each of us holds two of four roles: A drives and records, B runs the
  data and the research. The portal gained its twelve figures for each upload, one evaluation at a time, and a new
  upload becomes final only once it completes.
- **26 October.** The leaderboard ranks by PnL, not by a risk-adjusted score. The first disguised rehearsal ran the
  same day, and three more followed on 28 October, 30 October and 3 November (chapter 1). Each changed the plan: the
  third taught the template to count its orders still on their way and, once its engine fit turned out to be
  circular, made `calibrate` refuse any fit worse than 5%; the fourth tested that refusal on a portal that wasn't our
  engine.
- **2 November.** The last e-mail: no elimination, every team plays all four rounds; any AI tools allowed; nobody
  may sleep in the building, but the whole team may leave to rest.
- **4 November.** This chapter, and the field guide's version of it.

### The weekend

![The weekend and one round, as planned. The weekend from `ON_THE_DAY.md`'s timeline, the round from `RUNBOOK.md`'s
"Each round"; both drawn from those files by `make_data.py`.](../figures/f14_timeline.png){#fig-timeline
fig-alt="Top: Saturday 8:00 registration, then the opening, the workshop, a playground from 10:30 to 12:00, lunch, then four five-hour rounds at 13:00, 19:00, 01:00 and 07:00, weighted 10, 20, 30 and 40 percent. Bottom: one round from T to T plus 5 hours, with the data at T, a validated upload by T plus 2 hours, and the strategy frozen half an hour before the deadline."}

Saturday starts with registration at 08:00, as a whole team. The Technical Rules are published at the opening, and
the *playground*, 10:30 to 12:00, is planned as the one chance to try the real exchange before anything is
scored. Then four
rounds, at 13:00, 19:00, 01:00 and 07:00 (@fig-timeline). The site's code weights them 10, 20, 30 and 40%, but no page
uses those weights, and the leaderboard it does show is per round, with no total: how the rounds combine is unknown
until the rules say [(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "Known so far" and "The day: timeline and roles")]{.src}.

### The morning: settle what changes the code

RUNBOOK's morning is about the answers that change code, before any strategy. One person reads the Technical Rules in
full and writes each answer into the "First hour" section of ON_THE_DAY: the entry point, the data format, whether orders
rest, the limits, the Python version, the time limit, the submission cap. Any module the organisers hand out goes into
the plug-in unchanged. In the playground three tracks run at once: a probe bot that measures the exchange's rules, the
data loader, and the bot's adapter. Over lunch, the first upload's figures go into calibrate.

The reason is the rehearsals. In the second and third, most of the time went on mapping the rules onto the engine and
writing the adapter, and the third's first upload lost its money to the adapter, not to the strategy (chapter 1). Chapter 2 is the
list of what can differ: whether orders rest, how the limit is enforced, what the data looks like.

### Why each round runs as it does

RUNBOOK's "Each round" is chapter 1's loop with times on it. Each step has its reason in this book:

- **The data and the rules first, then `diagnose` and the premise test** (T+0:00 to T+0:15): before tuning anything,
  find out what kind of market each product is (chapters 3, 5 and 7). Where a product behaves like an agent market
  rather than like Prosperity, a bot that does nothing is the benchmark [(`KICKOFF_PROMPT.md`, round 1, step
  5)]{.src}.
- **The grid under two fill models** (T+1:00): until the playground or the rules settle which fill model the Arena
  has, a choice must hold under both (chapters 10 and 11). A setting changes only to the grid's `pick`, with the one
  exception RUNBOOK names for round 1 if the total turns out to be raw PnL.
- **Stress, and a loss stop sized from it** (T+1:30): a loss stop about three times the bot's plain drawdown limits
  the damage when the market stops behaving like its data (chapters 7 and 13).
- **A validated bot, at least as good as the last one, uploaded by T+2:00:** its portal score against our backtest
  is the engine's error, and no two variants closer than that error can be told apart (chapter 12).
- **Stop changing the strategy half an hour before the deadline,** or earlier if twice the first evaluation's time
  is longer: the last change has the least evidence behind it, and an upload that fails can't be marked final.
- **The handover note ten minutes before the deadline:** what was learned, for the next round's session, which starts
  fresh. Chapter 1's rehearsal wrote one; the Arena's four are what this chapter's boxes will be written from.

### The rules that hold all day

Above every step sit RUNBOOK's "Rules that hold all day". Never upload code `arena.validate` hasn't passed, and never
a `GRAY_AREA` bot without an organiser's yes (chapter 9). A round's first upload is a bot that has already run in the
playground, or last round's final bot, because the validator checks only against our copy of their interface. Never
choose between two variants by a portal score that differs by less than the engine's error. One evaluation at a time,
and an upload that completes becomes final, so mark the chosen one final again after any exploratory upload. Naps
only in rounds 2 and 3, and only when the round looks like the one before. Each rule is a lesson from somewhere in
this book, written down so that nobody has to remember it at four in the morning.

### Each round, choose again

The site promises "a forgiving market" first and "a sophisticated finale". So the round-1 bot is a starting point
for round 2, not a default: RUNBOOK has each round re-run the premise test, re-grid every setting on the round's own
data, and try one alternative to the last round's approach by T+1:00. Every number in this book before the event was
measured on someone else's market: Prosperity's, our simulator's, ABIDES's or a rehearsal's. Each is a prior, to be
tested again on the Arena's data, round by round.

### Risk, once there is a score to protect

Two things decide how much risk to carry into the later rounds, and neither was known on 4 November: how the four
rounds combine into the final ranking, and whether profit carries over. The plan has the decision made in writing at
breakfast, before round 4, from `experiments.day.standings`: our rank under each way the rounds might combine, given
the standings and our round-4 grid [(`RUNBOOK.md`, "Rules that hold all day")]{.src}. If rounds 2 and 3's private
runs strayed from our backtests, a bot that sends nothing is on the list. The 2024 story is the frame: once you are
ahead, the variance you could avoid counts for more than it did, and when you are behind, for less (chapter 13).

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
A competition ranked on one final evaluation rewards the probability of being first, not the expected score, the way
a leaderboard with a private test set rewards robustness over the public score. Where the analogy breaks: on a
leaderboard you choose the model once, while here the stake can change from round to round, after you have seen the
standings, so the choice of risk is itself a decision made on new information. And the rounds may not be the same
task: the organisers promise harder ones, so a model fitted to round 1 is a prior for round 2, not a solution.
:::
